summary: This specification lets an HTTP response be tagged with one or more strings, forming groups of stored responses in a cache. Caches can then treat related responses together, for example to invalidate them as a group.

plainLanguage.summary: Put sticky labels on saved items so you can throw out every item with the same label at once. HTTP caches can do this for web pages.

questions: how do i invalidate related cached responses
subtitle: Tag HTTP responses with group names so a cache can drop related stored responses together.

tldr.problem: HTTP caches treat every stored response on its own, so there is no dedicated way to say that a set of resources is related and should be invalidated together.
tldr.mechanism: A server adds a Cache-Groups header listing opaque strings. Stored responses from one origin that share a string are in the same group. A Cache-Group-Invalidation header on a response to an unsafe request names groups whose members may be invalidated.
tldr.outcome: Caches MAY invalidate grouped responses, so the mechanism is permissive unless a cache extension strengthens it. It works within one cache and one origin and does not cascade.

today: RFC 9875 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Group Cached Responses
sections.content:
HTTP caching, defined in RFC 9111, works on one resource at a time. The freshness of one stored response does not affect any other. That is efficient when a page is built from many assets with different caching needs.

Sometimes the relationship between responses matters. A state-changing request can have side effects on other resources, or an operator may just want to "invalidate this part of the site". Cache groups give a dedicated way to express those relationships instead of relying on URL structure. The RFC also notes that groups could inform cache eviction algorithms.

The scope is narrow. The mechanisms work within a single cache, across the stored responses of a single origin server. They do not synchronise state between caches in a hierarchy or mesh, and they do not link responses from different origins.
sections.plainLanguage: A web cache keeps copies of pages, but each copy is on its own. This idea lets the website say which copies belong together so they can be cleaned out together.

sections.title: The Cache-Groups Header Field
sections.content:
The Cache-Groups response header field is a List of Strings in the Structured Fields format. Each member names a group the response belongs to. The strings are opaque: they may mean something to the server that creates them, but the cache cannot see any structure in them beyond using them to identify a group.

An example from the RFC is a script response carrying Cache-Groups: "scripts" next to Cache-Control: max-age=3600.

The order of members does not matter, and unrecognised Parameters are ignored. Implementations MUST support at least 32 groups in a field value, with up to at least 32 characters in each member. General limits on HTTP field length may restrict the field in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: The website writes one or more label words on each page it sends. The cache does not need to understand the words. It only needs to know which pages have the same word.

sections.title: Who Is in the Same Group
sections.content:
Two responses stored in the same cache are in the same group only when both of these are true:

  • Both have a Cache-Groups field containing the same String, in any position, compared character by character and case sensitive.
  • Both share the same URI origin.

The origin condition means a group name is scoped to one origin. The string "scripts" on one site never ties together responses from another.
sections.plainLanguage: Two saved pages are in the same club only if they wear the exact same label and also come from the same website.

sections.title: Invalidation Behaviour
sections.content:
When a cache invalidates a stored response, it MAY also invalidate any stored responses that share a group with it. The word is MAY, so a cache is allowed but not forced to do this. The mechanism does not cascade: an invalidation caused by grouping does not trigger further grouped invalidations.

Cache extensions can make this stricter. The RFC gives the example of a targeted cache control header field (RFC 9213) that requires caches processing it to invalidate such responses.

The second header, Cache-Group-Invalidation, is also a List of Strings. Each member names a group that the response invalidates. For instance, the response to a POST with side effects on two groups could carry Cache-Group-Invalidation: "eurovision-results", "australia".

The field MUST be ignored on responses to requests with a safe method such as GET. A cache that receives it on a response to an unsafe request MAY invalidate stored responses sharing any of the listed groups. Extensions can strengthen that too. The same minimums apply as for the other field: at least 32 groups, with at least 32 characters per member.
sections.plainLanguage: When one saved page is thrown out, the cache may throw out its label-mates too. A website can also shout the label names after changing something, so the cache clears them. Only changes count, not simple looking.

sections.title: Shared Hosting Risk
sections.content:
Because resources that share an origin can invalidate each other, an origin that serves several parties (shared hosting) could let one party put its resources in another's groups or send signals that affect them.

The RFC's advice is that shared hosts wishing to reduce these risks can control access to the two header fields.
sections.plainLanguage: If many people share one notice board, one of them could use your label to make your notes get taken down. The board owner can decide who may use the labels.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA has added two entries to the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Field Name Registry: Cache-Groups and Cache-Group-Invalidation. Both have status permanent and reference RFC 9875.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of header names now includes the two new ones, so nobody else will use those names for something different.
